opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so if you look at the history of reinforcement learning, the algorithms themselves have actually been fairly robust for a while. Policy gradient methods, things like PPO, the core machinery works. When you look at the big successes, AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and more recently reasoning models trained on math and code, what they all have in common is a really clean, reliable reward signal. In Go you either win or you lose. In math you either get the right answer or you don't. In code the unit tests pass or they fail.

The problem is that most of what we actually care about in the real world doesn't look like that. If you want an agent to do a useful piece of knowledge work, write a good analysis, navigate a messy enterprise codebase, or make a judgment call, there's no ground truth checker sitting there telling you "plus one" or "minus one." So the question becomes: where does the reward come from?

The obvious answer is to use a learned reward model, have a model judge the output. But the moment you optimize hard against a learned reward, the policy finds the cracks in it. That's reward hacking. The policy gets very good at pleasing the judge rather than actually doing the task. So you can scale compute on the policy side all you want, but you're capped by how faithful and robust your reward signal is.

That's why I think of it as the fundamental bottleneck. Pre-training scaled because the objective, next-token prediction, is essentially free and infinite. You have the whole internet. With RL, the analogous thing would be having rewards that are both accurate and abundant across a huge range of tasks, and we don't have that yet. Whoever figures out how to generate reliable reward signals at scale for open-ended tasks, through better verifiers, through grounding in real environments and real outcomes, or through some combination, is going to unlock the next big jump in capability. The algorithms are ready. The rewards are what's holding us back.

r001.rationale: The response says existing RL algorithms are robust and rewards are the bottleneck, but does not say that accurate rewards for arbitrary tasks would leave exploration as the main limitation.

r002.rationale: It says policies can exploit cracks in learned reward models, but does not claim noisy or stochastic rewards are inevitably exploited.

r003.rationale: It contrasts tasks with clean ground-truth rewards against open-ended tasks, but does not explain that learning from the limited ground-truth tasks depends on generalizing to others.

r004.rationale: The response does not suggest that a neural network able to accurately verify any outcome would probably be a superintelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so if you think about why reinforcement learning worked in the cases where it really worked, it almost always comes down to the reward. AlphaGo, Atari, Dota, all of those had a reward signal that was essentially free. The game tells you whether you won or lost. You can run millions of episodes and the environment just hands you a perfect, verifiable signal at the end. And when you have that, RL is incredibly powerful. You can scale compute and the agent keeps getting better, because there's nothing fuzzy about what "better" means.

The problem is that the moment you step outside of games and into the things we actually care about, that signal disappears. If I ask a model to write a good research summary, or plan a trip, or refactor a codebase, there's no scoreboard. Someone has to decide what good looks like. And the way the field dealt with that for a while was human feedback, RLHF, where you train a reward model on human preferences. That works to a point, but it has two problems. One is that it's expensive and slow, you're bottlenecked on people. The other is that human preference is a pretty noisy, exploitable target. The policy learns to produce things that look good to a reward model rather than things that are actually good, and you hit a ceiling fast.

So the way I think about it is that compute and algorithms are not really the constraint anymore. We know how to do policy gradient at scale, we know how to do search. What we don't have, for most domains, is a reward that is dense enough, accurate enough, and cheap enough to let you turn the compute crank. That's why you see the big recent wins concentrated in math and code. Those are the domains where you can verify the answer, run the tests, check the proof. The reward is basically back to being a game score.

The interesting question is how you extend that to everything else. And I think the answer is that you have to treat reward construction as a first-class research problem, not an afterthought. You want models that can evaluate work, break down a long-horizon task into pieces you can actually check, and generate signal in domains where there's no unit test. If you can crack that, you unlock RL for the whole long tail of knowledge work. If you can't, you're stuck in the handful of domains that happen to come with a verifier built in.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling depends on having dense, accurate, cheap rewards, but it does not say that exploration would be the main limit even if accurate rewards existed.

r002.rationale: It describes human preferences as noisy and exploitable, but does not claim that noisy or stochastic rewards inevitably lead to reward hacking.

r003.rationale: It notes that math and code have verifiable rewards, but does not say that optimizing on those tasks depends on generalizing to other tasks.

r004.rationale: It proposes models that can evaluate work, but does not say that a neural network capable of accurately verifying any outcome would probably be a superintelligence.

astra-6.text:
Because reinforcement learning needs a signal that tells it whether what it did was good. You can give a model more compute, let it try more things, generate more experience—but unless you can reliably score those attempts, you don’t necessarily get a better model. You get a model that’s better at maximizing whatever signal you gave it.

With pretraining, that signal is essentially built into the data: predict the next token, and the text tells you what the answer was. With reinforcement learning, you have to supply that feedback. And for a lot of the things we want models to do, evaluating success is itself a hard problem.

Code is a useful example. If you have good tests, the model can try a solution, run it, see what failed, and improve. That gives you a loop you can scale. But if you ask a model to develop a research idea or carry out a complicated task, what’s the equivalent of the test? Can you evaluate the outcome accurately, cheaply, and without the model finding a shortcut that gets a high score without actually doing what you wanted?

So the bottleneck isn’t just generating more attempts. It’s building feedback that stays meaningful as the model gets better. Wherever you can do that, you have a path to scaling reinforcement learning.

r001.rationale: The response says reliable scoring enables scalable RL, but does not say that accurate rewards for arbitrary tasks would leave exploration as the main limit for simple RL methods.

r002.rationale: It warns that a model might find a shortcut to a high score, but does not claim noisy or stochastic rewards are inevitably exploited.

r003.rationale: It contrasts tasks with good tests against harder-to-evaluate tasks, but does not explain that training on tasks with ground-truth rewards relies on generalizing to other tasks.

r004.rationale: It discusses the difficulty of evaluating outcomes, but does not suggest that a neural network able to verify any outcome would probably be a superintelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is, reinforcement learning lets a model learn from experience, but only if it can tell whether that experience was successful. You need a signal that says, “This was better than that.” And getting that signal reliably, across all the things we want models to do, is really hard.

In a game, the reward is built in. You win or you lose, you get a score. You can generate more experience, evaluate it, and keep improving. But if you ask a model to do research or complete a complicated task for you, what’s the equivalent of the score? Often, evaluating the result takes substantial human judgment. Sometimes you don’t know whether it was good until much later.

You can train another model to judge, but then you have to ask how reliable that judge is. If its judgment has a systematic flaw, reinforcement learning creates pressure to exploit that flaw. You can end up improving the measured reward without improving the behavior you actually care about.

So the bottleneck is: can we build reward signals that are cheap enough to scale, accurate enough to trust, and broad enough to cover useful tasks? If we can, then more computation and more experience become a powerful way to improve models. Without that, we don’t have a reliable direction to optimize in.

r001.rationale: The response says reliable, broad reward signals would let more computation and experience improve models, but it does not say that simple RL methods would then be limited primarily by exploration.

r002.rationale: It says a judge with a systematic flaw can be exploited, but does not claim noisy or stochastic rewards are inevitably exploited through reward hacking.

r003.rationale: It discusses evaluating a range of tasks, but does not explain that training on tasks with ground-truth rewards depends on generalizing to other tasks.

r004.rationale: It suggests training another model to judge and asks whether that judge is reliable, but does not suggest that a neural network able to verify any outcome would probably be superintelligent.
